idiom_name: factory returns std::unique_ptr (ownership transfer in the return type)
implementation_notes: The default realization and this file's summary: a factory returns std::unique_ptr<T> - exclusive ownership in the return type, move-only so ownership cannot be duplicated by accident, no overhead beyond the pointer, with std::make_unique (C++14) closing the raw-new gap. Choose it whenever the client is the single owner, which is the common case; switch to std::shared_ptr<T> when sharing is real (control block plus atomic refcount, and safe deletion through a base without a virtual destructor), and to std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter when the resource is borrowed and the release must hand it back to its owner instead of deleting it. C++11 move semantics make the exclusive form the default recommendation; std::unique_ptr::release()/raw-pointer extraction are the escape hatches to keep out of published interfaces.
pitfalls: unique_ptr<T> converts implicitly to unique_ptr<B>, and the default deleter then deletes through B - undefined behaviour unless B has a virtual destructor.
Constructing two owners from one raw pointer, or keeping the raw pointer from release(), produces a double delete or a leak; return the wrapper and keep the raw handle private.

variants.name: Shared ownership: factory returns std::shared_ptr
variants.implementation_notes: Return std::shared_ptr<T> when the resource must really be shared (caches, observer lists, values stored in several containers) or when deletion through a base pointer must work without a virtual destructor, because the control block remembers the original type and deleter. Cost: a control block, atomic reference counting and a later, less predictable release; keep-alive cycles leak until they are broken. When the deleter hides a hand-back, the last release is what returns the resource to its owner, so the owner observes the return only when the final reference goes away.
pitfalls: Reference cycles (objects holding shared_ptr to each other, or a session holding its registry) keep the resource alive and never hand it back; use weak_ptr for back-references.
shared_ptr pays a control block and atomic traffic per hand-over; defaulting every factory to shared ownership hides the ownership decision instead of making it.

variants.name: Custom release policy: unique_ptr with a deleter that hands the resource back
variants.idiom_name: std::unique_ptr<T, Deleter> with a pool/owner check-in deleter
variants.implementation_notes: When the resource is borrowed from an owner, the deleter - not the client - must perform the hand-back: a function object that calls pool.checkin()/unref()/return-back instead of delete. This is the direct C++ realization of 'handed back rather than closed', and it keeps the destroy path unreachable from client code; the deleter is part of the type, so the return type itself spells out the release policy. The user-defined Handle/Body wrapper from the canonical idiom remains the answer when the release needs a bespoke protocol (custom handle type, shared memory, offset pointers) - unique_ptr supports any NullablePointer handle plus a custom deleter for exactly that case.
pitfalls: A deleter that captures a manager pointer must not outlive that manager: a Loan kept past the pool's destruction turns scope exit into a use-after-free.
Types mix: Loan and std::unique_ptr<Conn> are incompatible return types even though both own a Conn; the release policy is part of the type, so pick one wrapper per API and stay with it.
